crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
children.blurb: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance is an assurance review of whether a finance function can adopt AI tools without breaking controls, reporting integrity, or data protection.

children.name: Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models
children.blurb: Keeping financial data out of public models covers the controls and practices that stop sensitive financial information from being entered into, retained by, or used to train AI services that are open to the public.

children.name: Model Risk and Bias Testing
children.blurb: Model risk and bias testing covers the controls used to find, measure and limit harm from models that make or inform financial decisions.

children.name: Mapping Financial AI to the Rules
children.blurb: Mapping financial AI to the rules means taking every AI system used in finance, from credit scoring to fraud detection to customer service, and tying it to the specific laws, regulations, and internal policies that apply.

children.name: Local and Air-Gapped Deployment
children.blurb: Local and air-gapped deployment covers running AI models, data pipelines, and supporting services on hardware the organization controls, either inside its own network or on a physically isolated network with no route to the public internet.

sections.body: Governance, risk and financial data security is the part of AI accounting that keeps machine learning from turning into an uncontrolled ledger. In practice, finance teams are running enablement audits before they let staff use generative tools, checking which systems touch client data and which do not. They are also testing models for bias and drift, mapping AI use to existing rules, and choosing local or air-gapped deployment when data cannot leave the building. The work is operational, not theoretical: it involves access logs, data classification, prompt reviews, vendor questionnaires and model validation reports. AI is doing the same tasks it does elsewhere, predicting, classifying and generating text, but here the output can affect financial statements, audit opinions and regulatory filings. The goal is not to stop AI use, it is to make that use visible, bounded and reviewable.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The field is partly solved at the level of basic controls. Identity management, encryption, data loss prevention and private model hosting are mature enough for many finance functions. What is not solved is assurance. Bias testing in finance is still young, and a test that passes today may not hold when data shifts or a vendor updates a model. Regulatory mapping is fragmented across jurisdictions, and the atlas tracks 222 compliance and regulation pages, which reflects how many overlapping rules exist. Data leakage remains a live problem because a single prompt can move confidential figures into a public model, and logging every prompt at scale is hard. Model risk teams can document what a model does, but they often cannot fully explain why it produced a specific number, especially with third-party systems. Air-gapped deployment reduces exposure but also limits access to the newest capabilities, so it is a trade-off rather than a cure.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages in this section form a sequence from readiness to containment to validation to compliance to infrastructure. The AI Enablement Audit in Finance is the entry point for a team asking what AI is already in use and what controls are missing. Keeping Financial Data Out of Public Models then addresses the specific risk of confidential information leaving through prompts, plugins or connected tools. Model Risk and Bias Testing covers how to check whether a model is stable, fair and fit for a financial task, and what evidence a reviewer should expect. Mapping Financial AI to the Rules connects those controls to regulatory obligations and reporting duties, while Local and Air-Gapped Deployment explains how to run models in restricted environments when data cannot be sent to an external service. A reader would go to the audit page for a baseline, the leakage page for data boundaries, the testing page for validation methods, the mapping page for rule coverage, and the deployment page for architecture choices.
